To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“Carcass yield is a heritable trait with high genetic gain potential and is positively correlated with head size, which is a predictor of the yield of fillets, but not negatively correlated with the latter.
carcass and fillets yields are heritable traits with moderate and high heritability, respectively, that are only poorly correlated.

1) carcass yield and fillet yield are moderately heritable and poorly correlated traits; 2) carcass yield is more accurately predicted than fillet yield; 3) carcass yield can be predicted from ultrasound and surface measurements; 4) fillet yield can be predicted with ultrasound measurements; 5) carcass yield increases and fillet yield decreases with relative head size.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the best morphological traits for indirect selection of carcass and fillets in European sea bass, which is a prerequisite for the implementation of a selective breeding program in this species.
the development of a breeding strategy to improve both fillet yield and total yield in sea bass.
a first approach to identify predictors for fillet and carcas yield, and to investigate their genetic relationships with fillet and carcasse yield.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best predictors are ultrasound measurements of the belly and the dorsal region.
ultrasound measurements of the body are promising for indirect selection of fillet and total yield.
carcass yield is highly heritable and could be improved by direct selection, whereas fillet yield is moderately heritable and could only be improved by indirect selection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

ultrasound measurements of the body and digital images can be used to predict carcass and fillets yield in European sea Bass, but that the accuracy of the prediction is rather moderate and that the predictors are not yet ready to be applied for selection.
carcass yield is a highly heritable trait and can be improved by selection.
the use of ultrasound and digital pictures to predict fillet and carcasses yield is possible, but the genetic improvement of these traits is limited by the lack of genetic correlation between them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ultrasound measurements are a good source of information for indirect individual selection of fillet and/or carcass yield in sea bass.
it is possible to improve the yield traits of European sea bass through selective breeding, but it requires a careful design of the predictors to use for indirect selection.
ultrasound measurements are promising predictors to improve fillet and carcasses yields in sea bass.
